stem: As one moves downward along a demand curve, absolute price elasticity will fall if…
answer: D is the familiar straight-line case, but B (downward and concave) also suffices under the usual interpretation. The item has more than one sufficient option.
solution: For inverse demandP(Q)>0 withP′<0, elasticity isε=−P/(QP′). Log differentiation givesε′/ε=P′/P−1/Q−P″/P′. If the inverse demand is concaveP″≤0, all terms are nonpositive and the first two strictly negative, so elasticity falls asQ increases. This covers a downward straight line as well. If “demand function” instead meansQ(P), concavity also givesdε/dP>0 and therefore decliningε asP falls. Hence merely downward slope is insufficient, and convexity does not guarantee the claim, but both B and D can support it.
hint: Differentiate elasticity, rather than confusing elasticity with slope.
notes: B and D are both sufficient for positive downward-sloping demand under standard smooth definitions; no unique MCQ key.
options: Downward sloping and a straight line

stem: Monopoly demandP=20−Q, costC=15+10Q. A lump-sum tax15 is imposed. What tax revenue is collected?
answer: Intended D:0 if the monopolist can avoid the levy and fixed costs by exiting. If the lump-sum tax is unavoidable, revenue is B:15.
solution: Without the levy, MR20−2Q equalsMC10 atQ5,P15, givingprofit75−65=10. A15 levy exceeds that profit, so if continued participation is voluntary and exit avoids all operating fixed commitments and the levy, the firm exits and tax revenue is0. If the levy truly must be paid independently of output or continued operation, it leaves the marginal output choice unchanged and yields government revenue15. If production fixed cost is sunk while the levy is avoidable, shutdown comparison also differs. The question does not state those incidence/exit rules, so the conditional distinction is required.
hint: Compute pretax profit and then ask whether shutdown avoids the tax.
notes: Tax avoidability and shutdown treatment of the fixed cost are unspecified; an unconditional answer would conceal a material assumption.

stem: On Christmas Eve a florist has unsold Christmas trees, originally costing5 each. Unsold trees are discarded at zero cost after that day. What pricing objective maximizes profit now?
answer: C:Choose a price maximizing total receipts.
solution: The purchase costs have already been incurred and cannot be changed by today’s sales. There is no salvage value and no disposal cost. Therefore today’s variable contribution equals revenue, and maximizing total receipts maximizes final profit. Selling every tree or keeping price above the historical cost5 need not maximize receipts.
hint: Ignore sunk acquisition costs in the current pricing decision.
options: Just low enough to sell every tree

stem: The open Keynesian model hasC=a+bY, autonomousG,I,X and importsM=.1Y. Which is necessarily false: MPC>1, MPC<1, .5<MPC<.7, or none of these?
answer: Under the conventional extra assumption0<b<1, A is false. The printed equations alone only requireb<1.1 for positive equilibrium and do not rule out1<b<1.1.
solution: Goods equilibrium isY=a+bY+G+I+X−.1Y, soY=(a+G+I+X)/(1.1−b). With positive autonomous spending, positiveY requiresb<1.1, not necessarilyb<1. The standard psychological assumption0<b<1 would makeA the intended answer, but it is not explicitly printed. For exampleb1.05 gives a positive, stable expenditure slope b−.1=.95 whileMPC exceeds1. Thus under the displayed algebra none ofA,B,C is necessarily false. The choice depends on whether the standard additional MPC bound is intended.
hint: Separate an assumed MPC restriction from a condition derived from the displayed equations.
notes: The source does not explicitly impose0<b<1; conventional textbook and literal-equation readings differ.

stem: (a) Marginal cost isMC(Q)=a+bQ+cQ², witha,b,c>0. DeriveAVC and describeMC/AVC in one diagram. (b) Productionq=xy and both input prices1. If minimized cost is4, findq.
answer: (a) AVC=a+(b/2)Q+(c/3)Q², increasing and belowMC forQ>0. (b) q4.
solution: (a) Variable cost is the integral from0 toQ ofMC: VC=aQ+(b/2)Q²+(c/3)Q³. Divide byQ to getAVC. Both curves start at vertical intercepta and rise convexly. Their difference is(b/2)Q+(2c/3)Q²>0 for positive output. MC therefore lies aboveAVC; with all coefficients positive there is noU-shaped minimum away from zero. (b) ByAM–GM, costx+y≥2√(xy)=2√q, attained atx=y. Set minimized cost4 to getq4 and input demandsx=y2.

stem: A short-run monopolist operates two plants withTC₁=ax₁²+bx₁+c andTC₂=ax₂²+dx₂+e, all coefficients positive. Both plants produce at the optimum. Show that the higher-output plant has lower average variable cost.
answer: At the common marginal costm, AVCᵢ=m−axᵢ, so higherxᵢ means lowerAVCᵢ.
solution: Optimal allocation of a given total output equalizes plant marginal costs:2ax₁+b=2ax₂+d=m (also equal to the monopoly’s marginal revenue). Plant1AVC=ax₁+b=m−ax₁; plant2AVC=ax₂+d=m−ax₂. Sincea>0, ifx₁>x₂ thenAVC₁<AVC₂, and conversely. Fixed costsc,e have no role in these variable-cost comparisons.
hint: Express each linear cost coefficient using the common marginal cost.

stem: Project1 costs1000 now and pays100 per year forever from next year. Project2 costs2000 now and also pays100 per year forever from next year. Draw investment demand in rupees for all market interest rates.
answer: For independent projects: investment3000 if0<r<5%;1000 if5%<r<10%;0 ifr>10%. At the cutoff rates the respective project has zeroNPV.
solution: At positive interest r, each perpetual100 stream hasPV100/r. Project1 is profitable whenr<.10; project2 whenr<.05. If projects are independent and each can be undertaken once, invest in both below5%, only the first between5% and10%, and neither above10%. Thus the investment-demand graph is a downward step function, with horizontal quantity thresholds3000,1000,0. At5% investment can be1000 or3000 depending on whether the zeroNPV second project is chosen; at10% it can be0 or1000. At nonpositive rates the ordinary finite perpetuity formula fails, but both positive streams have unbounded undiscounted present value and both are attractive. If projects are mutually exclusive, project2 is dominated by project1 and the3000 step is absent; independence is therefore stated.
hint: Compare the perpetuity present value with each setup cost.
notes: The step-demand answer assumes independent one-time projects, not mutually exclusive alternatives.

stem: Poor people earn500/month and consume all. Middle-class people earn2000 and consume1500. Rich people earn10000 and consume80%. (a)20% of people are poor,50% middle class: find aggregate average propensity to save. (b) Equal numbers move poor→middle and middle→rich: what happens toAPS?
answer: (a) APS17/82≈20.732%. (b) It increases slightly under the stated class incomes and saving rules.
solution: Use income weights rather than averaging individual saving ratios. Per person in the initial population, income is.2·500+.5·2000+.3·10000=4100 and saving is.2·0+.5·500+.3·2000=850. HenceAPS850/4100=17/82. If fractionh moves on each ladder, poor share becomes.2−h, middle share stays.5, rich share becomes.3+h. New income is4100+9500h and saving850+2000h. The derivative of their ratio has numerator2000·4100−9500·850=125000>0, soAPS rises for feasible0<h≤.2. The incremental saving/income ratio2000/9500 is slightly above the initialAPS.
hint: Aggregate total saving divided by total income; middle-class population is unchanged by equal opposing flows.

stem: A shop offers either a fixed meal80g rice+50g dal for15, or freely chosen quantities at1 per10g rice and2 per10g dal. R chooses the fixed meal; S orders120g rice+15g dal, also costing15. (a) Describe indifference-curve diagrams. (b) With fixed-meal and rice prices unchanged but a higher dal price, must they change choices?
answer: R’s fixed meal remains optimal. S’s response is not uniquely determined from rationality alone; with a fixed15 food budget the old quantity bundle becomes unaffordable and must change.
solution: With rice horizontal and dal vertical, the à-la-carte15 budget is.1r+.2d=15. S’s choice(120,15) lies on it. The fixed-meal option(80,50) lies beyond that line because its à-la-carte cost18 exceeds15. Draw R’s highest attainable indifference curve through the package and S’s through the chosen line point. When dal price rises at fixed income and other prices, the à-la-carte opportunity set contracts while the package remains available. Since R chose the package from the larger old set, it remains a maximizer in the smaller new set. S’s old full bundle including any other consumption is no longer affordable at the same spending allocation; S may shift along the à-la-carte set or switch to the package. With a fixed15 budget devoted exclusively to food, S cannot retain(120,15). If other consumption can be reduced, the food quantities alone need not change: more information on preferences is needed.
hint: Use revealed preference for the unchanged package and distinguish a fixed food budget from total income.
notes: Source does not specify a fixed total food budget or preferences beyond rationality; the conditional answer avoids asserting a unique S response.

stem: A consumer hasU(x₁,x₂)=x₁x₂, income650 and pricesp₁8,p₂2. Club membership lowers only good1’s price by50%. What is the maximum fee the consumer would just pay?
solution: Cobb–Douglas demands spend half of available income on each good, so indirect utility isM²/(4p₁p₂). Without the club it is650²/64. With feeF andp₁4 it is(650−F)²/32. Indifference requires(650−F)²=650²/2. Taking the positive available-income root gives650−F=650/√2, henceF=650−325√2. A smaller fee creates a strict gain.
hint: Equalize indirect utilities before and after paying the fee.
notes: Visual inspection confirms the scanned income isRs650, notRs600 as the broken text extraction suggests.

stem: A farmer owns1000 bushels now. Setting aside100 bushels yields110 next year. Utility isW=C₀C₁. With no capital market, how much should he consume in each year?
solution: Ifs bushels are planted or stored for the stated return, C₀1000−s andC₁1.1s. MaximizeW=1.1s(1000−s) over0≤s≤1000. Its derivative1.1(1000−2s) vanishes ats500, and the second derivative is negative. Therefore consume500 now and550 next year.
hint: Substitute the physical return into the intertemporal resource constraint.
notes: Only printed subpart(a) is included. A handwritten borrowing-at5% extension appears below it but is not treated as an official question or instruction.
